draft.title: Series circuits
card: In a series circuit, the components are connected one after another in a single loop. The charge has only one path to follow.
Current
is the same at every point in the loop, because charge is not used up and has nowhere else to go. I is the same through every component.
Voltage
is shared between the components. The voltages across them add up to the supply voltage: V = V1 + V2 + ...
Resistance
adds up. The total is R = R1 + R2 + ... and it is larger than any single resistor. Current then follows from I = V ÷ R.
draft.remember: In series, current is shared by all, while voltage and resistance add.

a.q: Two resistors are connected in series to a 12 V supply. The voltage across one is 5 V. What is the voltage across the other?
a.why: In series the voltages across the components add up to the supply voltage, so the other resistor has 12 - 5 = 7 V. It is not 5 V, because that would only be so if the resistors were equal, and we are not told that.
a.clue: The voltages must add up to the supply.

b.q: A 4 ohm resistor and a 8 ohm resistor are in series with a 6 V supply. What is the current through the 4 ohm resistor?
b.why: The total resistance is 4 + 8 = 12 ohm, so I = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 A. The same current flows through every component in series. 1.5 A comes from dividing the supply by the 4 ohm resistor alone, which ignores the other resistor.
b.clue: Add the resistances first, then use I = V ÷ R.

problems.detail: "Current is shared by all" can be read as current being divided between components. That contradicts the card, which says current is the same at every point, and the card uses "shared" for voltage. It should say current is the same everywhere.

The why says 5 V across the other resistor would be right if the resistors were equal. That is false: equal resistors on a 12 V supply would each have 6 V. 5 V is impossible here because 5 + 5 is not 12.
